hundred billion dollars in a single morning,
and it hadn't done anything wrong.
Nobody had.
No bank failed.
No law passed.
The economy looked fine.

The short answer is an election, six hundred thousand chips stuck in Hong Kong,
and some very rich people locking in a very good year.

California.

By late October, investors were staring at four cracks.
Crack one: the money goes in a circle.
Nvidia invests in its own customers,
the AI labs and chip-rental firms that then buy Nvidia chips.
It owns a stake in CoreWeave, which rents those chips out,
and agreed to buy up to six point three billion dollars of the computing power
CoreWeave can't sell.
Nvidia's own finance chief knows how that sounds: "we know some will call this
circular financing."
Here's a few billion dollars.
Wow!
What should I spend it on?
Funny you should ask.
Crack two: the chips are the collateral.
Firms like CoreWeave borrowed huge sums to buy chips, rented them out,
and pledged those same chips to borrow more.
At one point CoreWeave owed over five dollars for every dollar of equity.
Fine, while a used chip holds its value.
But Nvidia brings out a new generation every year or two,
and each one makes the last one worth less.
And Michael Burry, who called the housing crash,
says the giants book their servers as lasting longer than they do,
which flatters profits.
The nightmare: one borrower misses one
payment, the lender grabs the chips to sell,
and everyone learns that afternoon what a used AI chip is worth in a hurry.
It hasn't happened.
But every chip investor has thought about it.
Crack three: who's paying.
By the end of July,
Nvidia was owed about sixty-three billion dollars for chips it had shipped but not
been paid for yet.
And this year, just three buyers made up more than two fifths of its sales.
Picture a restaurant where three tables order two of every five plates,
and a lot of the food goes on a tab.
Crack four: the plug.
You can buy a chip.
You can't buy electricity that doesn't exist.
In northern Virginia, the data-center capital of the world,
the wait to hook a new building up to the grid had stretched to about seven years.
And the power that does exist, somebody pays for.
On America's biggest grid, across thirteen states,
power plants get paid just to stand ready, and families cover that in their bills.

than in twenty twenty-four, and the grid's own watchdog blamed data centers first.

It doesn't.
Around seventy million Americans save in a 401(k),
mostly through the same index funds,
and the pensions of teachers and firefighters hold them too.
When the seven giants fall, they fall too.
It goes deeper than stocks.
Data centers run on borrowed money,
much of it raised from insurers and pension funds.
Pimco bought a big piece of the bonds for Meta's giant Louisiana data center with

some making two hundred and sixty thousand dollars a year on data-center jobs,

Thursday didn't stop that work.

I just didn't want the bill.

A market that's one-third AI had been sliding for a month.
Then, in three days, voters elected a Congress that might rein in data centers,
Beijing left six hundred thousand chips at the door,
and funds sitting on a great year cashed out.
Nothing broke.

It isn't new, either.
In the eighteen-forties, Britain went mad for railways,

Railway shares lost nearly two thirds of their value,
and a third or more of the approved lines never got built.

Not yet.
Both tariff-crash days in April twenty twenty-five were bigger,

A call, not a bill.

It was the day the market noticed there's a pin, and that voters,
Washington and Beijing all have a hand on it.
